title: "Catriona O"
---

Your exploratory data analysis of the team datasets go here.


```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

glaciers <- read.csv("../data/processed/glaciers.csv")
```


```{r}
head(glaciers)
dim(glaciers)
```

# Histogram of Mean Elevation

```{r}
ggplot(glaciers, aes(mean_elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "steelblue", color = "white")
```

> Most glaciers sit between about 500 and 2,500 m, peaking around 1,000 to 1,500 m, with a long right tail of a few very high ones up to roughly 4,000 m or more.


# Density of Median Elevation

```{r}
ggplot(glaciers, aes(median_elevation)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5)
```

> The distribution is right-skewed with a main peak near 900 m and a smaller bump around 1,600 m, which hints at more than one population of glaciers (probably different regions). There’s also a small secondary bump near 3,400 m.

# Boxplot of Elevation by UTM zone

```{r}
ggplot(glaciers, aes(factor(utm_zone), median_elevation)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue")
```

> Median elevation varies a lot by zone, rising steadily from about 1,000 m in zones 1-4 up to about 3,600 m in zone 13, then dropping to a lower, flatter range in zones 15-28. Zones 5-11 have lots of high outliers, and zone 14 is a single flat line, probably just one glacier.


# Map Colored By Mean Elevation

```{r}
ggplot(glaciers, aes(center_longitude, center_latitude)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = area_km2, color = mean_elevation, alpha = 0.4)) +
  coord_quickmap()
```

> The data covers Alaska/western Canada and the Arctic (Greenland and the Canadian Arctic), and the highest-elevation glaciers (lighter blue) are clustered in the southern Rockies and Sierra region around 35-45°N. Northern glaciers are almost all dark, meaning low elevation.
